Lessons.Title: Answer Questions about Scaled Bar Graphs
ExplanationParagraphs: First-edition 2021 Illustrative Mathematics K–5, Grade 3 Unit 1 Lesson 7, CCSS 3.MD.B.3. The original goal is to use SCALED bar graphs to solve one-step HOW MANY MORE and HOW MANY FEWER comparison problems within 100, by reading graph categories and using addition/subtraction or counting on. Source timeline: 10-minute How Many Do You See warm-up, 15-minute Favorite Time of Year problems, 20-minute Bugs in the Garden problems, 10-minute lesson synthesis, five-minute original Favorite Sports Cool-down. Edulytics text and figures are authored independently rather than copied from the publisher.

Warm-up — How Many Do You See? Groups of Dots (10 min). The 2021 original TWO dot images display seven and twenty-two dots. Explain the seven as three groups of two plus one, and the twenty-two as four groups of five plus two; alternative valid grouping strategies are welcome. Teacher flashes each image for 30 seconds quiet thinking, repeats pair discussion, and asks learners to explain and restate a partner's mental groups. An earlier first-party scaffold wrongly used 15 and 20 dots; that is corrected in the student view and must not be described as source equivalence.

Activity 1 — Questions about Favorite Time of Year (15 min). REUSE the actual learner-created graph from Lesson 6, with fixed public school survey values Winter 24, Spring 13, Summer 40, Fall 22. The original FOUR questions and exact answers: (1) how many students in all = 99; (2) how many chose Spring OR Fall = 35; (3) how many MORE chose Summer than Winter = 16; (4) how many FEWER chose Spring than Fall = 9. Students write expressions/equations, distinguish combining categories from comparing two, and discuss tens/ones strategies in pairs. The actual source graph of a particular pupil and peer discussion require teacher checking, not a numeric auto-pass.

Activity 2 — Questions About Bugs in the Garden (20 min). An independently authored vertical graph retains the original first-edition figure's 0–80 vertical axis by TENS and four approximate bar quantities inferred from official ALT data: Ants approximately 62, Ladybugs approximately 11, Beetles approximately 19, Spiders approximately 7. Source Student Facing has FIVE distinct parts: estimate total garden bugs (about 99), estimate Ant minus Spiders (the public teacher sample gives 53, while ALT integer interpretation gives 55), estimate Ant minus Ladybugs (about 51), WRITE TWO distinct answerable bug-graph questions and exchange those questions with another group and ANSWER theirs. Every approximate numerical answer is teacher-reviewed because the original source explicitly accepts different reasonable estimates; the provisional near-number helper is NEVER the pass authority. Numbered group/partner steps and MLR8 teacher supports are separate from computed answers.

Lesson synthesis (10 min) happens BEFORE the source Cool-down; ask about strategies for reading bars between tens, counting on and selecting addition versus subtraction. Original SOURCE Cool-down — Favorite Sports (5 min) shows Football 28, Soccer 61, Basketball 35, Hockey 22 on a vertical graph from 0–70 by 5. Two distinct source comparison prompts require 61−28=33 MORE Soccer than Football and 35−22=13 FEWER Hockey than Basketball; pupils write equations or expressions for both. These are NOT equivalent to the optional first-party fictional sports-club numerical drill. Independent Edulytics graph artwork preserves source numerical relationships without reproducing original copyrighted layout. Suggested teacher-led centers are Sort and Display Stage 3 and Five in a Row Stage 6.

KeyConcepts.Title: Read a scaled bar graph accurately
KeyConcepts.Definition: A bar's height is read relative to the labelled numerical axis, not the number of unmarked spaces alone.
KeyConcepts.Rule: With tens ticks, interpret in-between endpoints as approximate values; accept sensible visual variation.
KeyConcepts.Example: On the first-edition bugs chart ants are a little over 60 and spiders below 10; their difference is approximately mid-50s.

KeyConcepts.Title: One-step compare: how many more
KeyConcepts.Definition: How many more means subtract the smaller category from the larger category.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Write large − small and name the comparison in the answer.
KeyConcepts.Example: From previous season graph: Summer 40 minus Winter 24 equals 16 more.

KeyConcepts.Title: One-step compare: how many fewer
KeyConcepts.Definition: How many fewer is the same absolute category difference viewed from the smaller category.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Calculate the difference between the named categories, not their sum.
KeyConcepts.Example: Spring 13 is nine fewer than Fall 22, because 22−13=9.

KeyConcepts.Title: Combine versus compare
KeyConcepts.Definition: 'Spring OR Fall' combines nonoverlapping survey choices; 'Spring fewer than Fall' compares their counts.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use addition for the first type, subtraction for the second.
KeyConcepts.Example: 13+22=35 choosing Spring or Fall, versus 22−13=9 fewer Spring than Fall.

KeyConcepts.Title: Source-original Cool-down distinct from optional extra
KeyConcepts.Definition: The original 2021 Favorite Sports Cool-down has its own graph and two exact comparisons.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Grade the two original numerical differences separately, with teacher-reviewed expressions; keep fictional sports-club data optional.

WorkedExamples.Title: Warm-up — subitize 7 and 22
WorkedExamples.Question: How many dots are visible without counting each one?
Steps: See three pairs of dots and one more: 2+2+2+1.
Add six and one to get 7.
See four groups of five and two more: 5+5+5+5+2.
Add twenty and two to get 22; discuss alternative groupings with a partner.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 7 in the first image; 22 in the second.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source Activity 1 — four season graph problems
WorkedExamples.Question: Winter24, Spring13, Summer40, Fall22; solve all four first-edition source tasks.
WorkedExamples.Method: Distinguish total, OR addition and two comparisons.
Steps: For how many MORE Summer than Winter: 40−24=16.
For how many FEWER Spring than Fall: 22−13=9.
Explain tens-and-ones methods to a partner.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source Activity 2 — estimate with the bug graph
WorkedExamples.Question: A tens-scaled bug graph has Ants a little over 60, Ladybugs a little above 10, Beetles just under 20 and Spiders just under 10.
WorkedExamples.Method: First read visually reasonable approximate values; then choose arithmetic while retaining teacher acceptance of a range of estimates.
Steps: Read the four bar heights relative to 0–80 by tens, without pretending they have exact printed labels.
Find a reasonable total near 100 bugs.
Compare ants and spiders by subtracting a one-digit number from roughly sixty.
Compare ants and ladybugs similarly; record arithmetic and explain imprecision.
Invent two distinct new graph questions, exchange them with a peer group and answer theirs for teacher review.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Example estimates: approximately 99 total, around 53–55 more ants than spiders, about 51 fewer ladybugs than ants. Other reasonable visual estimates may be accepted.
WorkedExamples.Check: The public teacher guide expressly accepts reasonable variations; NOT auto-graded to fixed 99/55/51.

WorkedExamples.Title: 2021 original Favorite Sports Cool-down
WorkedExamples.Question: Soccer versus Football: how many more? Hockey versus Basketball: how many fewer?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use source four-category graph 0–70 with 5-unit ticks and two distinct one-step comparison equations.
Steps: Read Football 28, Soccer 61, Basketball 35 and Hockey 22 from the original numerical graph.
Record 13 students FEWER, with a supporting expression for the teacher.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 33 more soccer than football; 13 fewer hockey than basketball.
WorkedExamples.Check: 61−28=33;35−22=13; both equations and source graph reading separately teacher-reviewed.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using 15 and 20 as original 2021 warm-up dot totals.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The first-edition teacher-guide sample gives 7 and 22.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Present seven and twenty-two dots and allow multiple grouping justifications.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding Spring and Fall for a how-many-fewer question.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A difference asks how far apart two quantities are, not their combination.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Spring OR Fall uses 13+22; Spring fewer than Fall uses 22−13.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Rejecting a reasonable bug estimate because it differs from a fixed internal ALT-derived quantity.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Ticks are separated by ten and source openly accepts multiple reasonable estimates.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Require human teacher judgment for all three estimate questions and their explanations, never an auto-pass.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Ignoring the fifth bug activity part: exchanging new graph questions with another group.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Writing two questions alone does not fulfill the original partner interaction.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Record the distinct exchange/response as teacher-led; human classroom observation is separate from text.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Substituting the optional fictional club exercise for the publisher's Favorite Sports source Cool-down.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original 2021 two source comparisons ask Soccer−Football and Basketball−Hockey.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Show the independent rendering of original category values and evaluate 33 and 13, plus teacher-reviewed equations.

SummaryPoints: Warm-up 10 minutes: two source dot images have SEVEN and TWENTY-TWO dots; grouping and partner talk.
Activity1 15 minutes: reuse the L06 pupil graph, Winter24 Spring13 Summer40 Fall22; exact four answers 99,35,16,9 with equations.
Activity2 20 minutes: Bugs in Garden 0–80 in tens, reasonable teacher-judged estimates; two self-authored questions, then answers exchanged with another group.
Source synthesis 10 minutes BEFORE Cool-down: compare graph reading and addition/subtraction strategies.
Original Favorite Sports Cool-down 5 minutes: Football28 Soccer61 Basketball35 Hockey22 with 0–70 tick5, answer 33 and 13, show equations.
Optional Edulytics fictional sports-club numeric exercise is NOT source Cool-down; original images not reused and teacher-led centers remain teacher-led.
